quotes.text: Nightmares In Wax, the name under which Dead Or Alive originated, definitely has more in common with the UK post-punk scene – the Stock-Aitken-Waterman sheen of Dead Or Alive's biggest commercial hits is nowhere to be found.
This material has far more in common with Joy Division and The Cure than it does with Bronski Beat or Pet Shop Boys.

Even when Pete breaks into KC & The Sunshine Gang's "That's The Way (I Like It)" (which Dead Or Alive would more properly cover a couple years later on the Sophisticated Boom Boom album), it doesn't really have a disco sound to it.
"Girl Song" and "Shangri-La" feel like they owe more to The Doors than to the disco acts that they would come to resemble in their commercial peak.

The band would change their name to Dead Or Alive just in time for their next single, "I'm Falling." Again, the A-side of the single leans more toward Joy Division while the B-side, "Flowers," leans toward The Doors.
However, more than on the Nightmares In Wax single, Pete's vocals are starting to sound more like they would on the pop-oriented material.

"Flowers" even contains references to multiple songs from the sixties, including The Doors "The Crystal Ship," Pete Seeger's "Where Have All The Flowers Gone," and Jackie DeShannon's "What The World Needs Now Is Love."

In all honesty, I found this single to be the least interesting of these early releases. It isn't that it's bad material – it just feels like it's trying too hard to be different, with attempted Middle Eastern textures and other pretensions.
"It's Been Hours Now" is one of the strongest tracks on the first CD of this set to me. This is about the closest that this era of Dead Or Alive gets to the Sophisticated Boom Boom sound.

This new 3CD set, Let Them Drag My Soul Away: Singles, Demos, Sessions And Live Recordings 1979-1982, covers the evolution from post-punk goth-rock act Nightmares In Wax into the post-punk goth-pop act Dead Or Alive and hints at what would be coming as the band signed with Epic Records.

the strident Black Leather remains a stomping proto disco/post punk psychedelic gem as Burns recounts us with tales of how proudly he "rides big boys on motor bikes", which halfway through veers into K.C. & the Sunshine Band's That's the Way, which was a signpost for Burns future musical direction.

God Song continues the psych journey, across a stuttering beat and a simple keyboard, which allows Burns surprisingly strong baritone vocal to dominate, Shangri-La is another swirling collision of genres, jerky, angular, which these days could be considered a taster for much of the future post punk and goth sounds.

the track itself displayed a band more musically adept, they still had the raw edge evident in NIW, but had learnt how to utilise that power, Burns was more in control of his voice which sits lower in the mix whilst the keyboards led you through the proto-goth murk.
Personally, I always preferred the B-Side Flowers which leant heavily upon its Doors influences, though had enough of its own atmospheric identity to make this a vital release.

Similarly with Number 11 which was released in March 1981, complete with its glorious driving synth pattern atop of a propulsive rhythm that creates a simmering urgency, there is tension within Burns vocal as he demands to know "what's wrong with this world" as the track builds to an explosive conclusion.

The title tracks drum refrain, and the space allowed to the opening guitar chimes always remind me of similar period Sisters Of Mercy, though Dead Or Alive brought much more brooding warmth and through Burns voice an element of sexuality devoid from Leeds finest.

These tribal rhythms and mysticism were present in the pacey Nowhere To Nowhere complete with whipcracks which listening now effortlessly challenges the belief that DOA played gloomy almost turgid rock.

Personally, I always felt that the release was treading water, its more sombre atmospherics than the boundary pushing, though Burns delivers an assured vocal performance, whilst the flipside Some Of That relied upon tribal drumming as a platform for a repeated guitar refrain, whilst synth melodies wash around, and a husky Burns vocal simmers.

Even in their early days, Dead or Alive always had one eye on the dancefloor and I have many happy memories of hurling myself around various clubs to the Misty Circles twelve inch, so it did not come as much of a surprise when this element came even further to the fore.
First album, Sophisticated Boom Boom, was a record that managed to appeal to post punk kinds and pop kids, but soon all traces of punk influence was jettisoned for pure pop.
Second album Youthquake was relentlessly pop. Fashioned in the post Blue Monday world, it was robo-driven futurist pop at its most shiny and sparkly.
The track opens Youthquake, leading the way into an album of infectious and camp Hi NRG pop excess.

The album and single were produced by the fledgling Stock Aitken Waterman team and You Spin Me Round gave them their first number one record. It was not an easy relationship, with clashes reportedly getting close to physical violence. Regardless of that, both parties seemed to have benefitted from the collaboration.
The rest of Youthquake follows in a similar vein, being packed with high octane sequencer driven pop. There was shade in their palette though, as the likes of In Too Deep testify.
When it came to recording their fifth album, Dead or Alive, who were by this time known for their Hi-NRG, dancefloor hits, slowed things down… a little.
It's rare that an act comes along so fully formed that their first and last albums can be played together cohesively, but that's the case with Dead or Alive's debut.

Let's not overlook the enduring influence of their Top 40 version of That's The Way (I Like It), which undoubtedly influenced Stock Aitken Waterman's repertoire of cover versions in the following years.
Dead or Alive's '90s albums are often overlooked, but there's a treasure trove of standout tracks to be discovered, with 'Nukleopatra' a particularly impressive collection of techno gems.
The follow-up to UK Top 10 and US Top 40 LP 'Youthquake', the album is Dead or Alive's second record produced by Stock Aitken Waterman and sticks with the winning formula they hit on last time round.
'Youthquake', to this day, remains a seminal Hi-NRG album and, for those who dismiss Stock Aitken Waterman's musical legacy, a reminder of their forward-thinking productions.
